title: (Principal-level) You designed the system — what evidence would make you change your architecture? If you recommend Redis, explain what would convince you it is unnecessary. If you chose async messaging, explain what would make synchronous communication preferable. If you proposed microservices, identify which assumptions justify the boundaries — and why is an architecture much easier to trust when the engineer who designed it can also describe the conditions under which it becomes the WRONG architecture?
shortTitle: What evidence would make you change your architecture?

s1_definition.profdef: Every architectural choice rests on assumptions about load, latency, data volume, team structure, and failure modes, and each choice is correct only while those assumptions hold. A principal-level engineer can therefore state, for every major decision, the specific, measurable evidence that would invalidate it — the conditions under which the choice becomes wrong. Recommending Redis assumes a cache hit rate and read pattern that justify its operational cost; evidence that the hit rate is low or the data fits in the database's own cache would make it unnecessary. Choosing asynchronous messaging assumes the caller does not need an immediate authoritative result and can tolerate eventual consistency; evidence that the use case needs a synchronous answer with strong consistency would favour a synchronous call. Proposing microservices assumes independent scaling, deployment, and ownership boundaries that match real team and domain seams; evidence that the boundaries are arbitrary and coupling is high would favour a modular monolith. An architecture is far more trustworthy when its designer can articulate its own falsification conditions, because that proves the choice was reasoned from evidence rather than fashion, and it gives the organisation clear triggers to revisit the decision.
s1_definition.analogy: When the National Bank of India decides to open a new express counter, a good branch manager does not just say "express counters are good." They say "I am opening this because more than one in three customers only need a quick balance check; if that drops below one in ten, this counter is wasting a clerk and I will close it." That second sentence — the condition under which the decision becomes wrong — is what makes the manager trustworthy. Anyone can propose a shiny new counter; a senior manager tells you exactly what evidence would make them tear it down. The same is true for every big banking-technology choice: a fast-lookup cache, sending messages by courier instead of waiting on the phone, or splitting one big department into many small ones — each is right only under stated conditions, and a strong engineer names those conditions out loud.
s1_definition.oneliner: A trustworthy architecture comes with its own falsification conditions — the designer can state the measurable evidence that would make each choice wrong, which proves it was reasoned, not fashionable.

sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, an engineer has designed a system with three choices: Redis in front of the account balance reads, asynchronous messaging for notifications, and a split into separate transfer and account microservices. The leadership asks the principal-level question: what evidence would make each of these wrong.

Problem 1 — nobody has written down the assumptions, so there is no objective way to know if Redis is still earning its keep, if async is right for a given flow, or if the service split still matches the teams.

Problem 2 — without falsification triggers, these decisions calcify: Redis stays even when the hit rate collapses, async is used even where a synchronous answer is needed, and the service boundaries persist even when every feature requires coordinated deploys.

The fix encodes each decision as an assumption plus a measurable trigger, and a `DecisionReviewer` evaluates live metrics to report whether each choice is still justified or whether the evidence now says it is wrong. The mini-project builds `ArchitectureDecision` objects for Redis, async, and microservices, each with a predicate over metrics, and a demo that feeds healthy and then degraded metrics to show each decision flipping from justified to "should revisit" when its falsification condition is met.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: three architectural decisions — Redis, async messaging, microservices — each with an assumption and a falsification trigger, evaluated first against healthy metrics and then against degraded metrics.

Step 1 — Decisions registered with triggers. Each decision is stored not as a bare choice but as an assumption plus the measurable condition that would make it wrong: Redis needs a hit rate of at least fifty percent and database read utilisation of at least thirty percent; async needs the caller to tolerate eventual results; microservices need change-coupling at or below fifty percent.

Step 2 — First review, healthy evidence. The metrics show a ninety percent cache hit rate, seventy percent database read utilisation, eventual-consistency tolerance, and ten percent change-coupling. The reviewer evaluates each predicate, finds all satisfied, and reports all three decisions as justified, naming the assumption behind each.

Step 3 — Evidence degrades. New metrics arrive: the cache hit rate has collapsed to twenty percent and database read utilisation is ten percent, the business now needs an immediate authoritative result, and change-coupling has risen to eighty percent because most features require coordinated deploys across services.

Step 4 — Second review, falsification. The reviewer evaluates the same predicates against the degraded metrics. Redis fails because the hit rate and read utilisation are below their thresholds, so the cache is adding a hop without saving work. Async fails because the caller now needs an immediate result, so synchronous communication is preferable. Microservices fail because change-coupling exceeds fifty percent, meaning the boundaries no longer match reality and a modular monolith would be simpler.

Step 5 — Outcome. Each decision is reported as "should revisit," citing the exact falsification condition that the evidence now meets. The architecture did not become wrong by opinion; it became wrong by measurement, and because the triggers were written down in advance, the team has an objective basis to change course.

```
2026-10-24 19:34:50 [INFO] === Review 1: healthy evidence ===
2026-10-24 19:34:50 [INFO] Redis cache: JUSTIFIED (high hit rate + DB under read pressure)
2026-10-24 19:34:50 [INFO] Async messaging: JUSTIFIED (caller tolerates eventual result)
2026-10-24 19:34:50 [INFO] Microservices: JUSTIFIED (low change-coupling + separate teams)
2026-10-24 19:34:50 [INFO] === Review 2: evidence now says choices are wrong ===
2026-10-24 19:34:50 [WARNING] Redis cache: SHOULD REVISIT — evidence met falsify condition: hit rate < 0.5 OR db read util < 0.3
2026-10-24 19:34:50 [WARNING] Async messaging: SHOULD REVISIT — evidence met falsify condition: use case needs an immediate authoritative result
2026-10-24 19:34:50 [WARNING] Microservices: SHOULD REVISIT — evidence met falsify condition: change-coupling > 0.5 (features need coordinated deploys)
```

```
    │
    ▼ DecisionReviewer evaluates each predicate against live metrics
    ├─ Redis:   hitRate≥0.5 AND dbReadUtil≥0.3 ?
    ├─ Async:   toleratesEventual AND !needsImmediateResult ?
    └─ Micro:   changeCoupling≤0.5 ?

    ├─ healthy metrics → ALL JUSTIFIED
    └─ degraded metrics → each trigger met → SHOULD REVISIT

  Objective, measurable triggers → revisit the architecture by evidence, not opinion
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The thing that distinguishes principal-level architecture thinking is not how confidently I can defend a design, but how precisely I can describe what would prove it wrong. Every architectural choice is a bet on a set of assumptions about load, latency, data volume, team structure, and failure modes, and the choice is correct only while those assumptions hold. So for every major decision I make the assumptions explicit and attach a measurable trigger that tells the organisation when to revisit. That is why I can answer the three specific examples directly.

If I recommend Redis, I am assuming there is a hot set of data read far more often than it changes, that read volume is high enough that the database cannot comfortably serve it, and that the latency gain justifies operating a second data store with its own consistency and eviction behaviour. What would convince me Redis is unnecessary is evidence: a measured cache hit rate that is low, so most reads miss and hit the database anyway and the cache is just an extra hop; a database nowhere near its read capacity whose own buffer cache already serves the hot set; or a data set small enough that an in-process cache suffices. If I choose asynchronous messaging, I am assuming the caller does not need an immediate authoritative answer and can tolerate eventual consistency, and that decoupling producer and consumer is worth the broker's operational weight. What would make synchronous communication preferable is a use case that must have the result now to proceed, like a point-of-sale authorisation that must approve or decline before the customer leaves, or a strong-consistency requirement where acting on not-yet-processed state is unacceptable. And if I propose microservices, I am assuming independent scaling, deployment, and ownership, with boundaries drawn along genuine domain seams where cross-boundary coupling is low. What would tell me the boundaries are wrong is that most features require coordinated deploys across several services, or a single small team is drowning in the distributed-systems tax, or the services share data and couple through a database anyway — in which case a modular monolith gives the same separation without the overhead.

The reason an architecture is so much easier to trust when its designer can state these falsification conditions is threefold. First, it proves the decision was reasoned from evidence and requirements rather than copied from a conference talk, because only a reasoned decision has identifiable assumptions. Second, it gives the organisation concrete, measurable triggers — a hit rate below a threshold, change-coupling above a threshold, a latency requirement that flips — so the decision can be revisited objectively instead of through politics or inertia. Third, it builds trust, because an engineer who volunteers the weaknesses of their own design is demonstrably reasoning honestly rather than selling.

In my banking work I treat every significant choice as an architecture decision record that pairs the assumption with the condition that would invalidate it, and I review those conditions against live metrics on a cadence. The deepest version of this is that good architecture is not a permanent truth; it is a time-bound fit to current constraints, and part of my job as the designer is to mark the expiry conditions so the system evolves deliberately as the evidence changes, rather than ossifying until it breaks. So when an interviewer asks what would make me change my architecture, the honest and senior answer is a specific, measurable list — and the fact that I can produce that list is exactly what should make them trust the design in the first place.
